title: Laporte Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Laporte wells have a 40 ft median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling cost and water supply highly variable.
h1: What Laporte Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well records around Laporte show a wide range of conditions. The median reported depth is 40 feet, but the middle half of wells runs from 21 to 118 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,340 feet. Most permits are for domestic or household use, and most wells are identified with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers.

That combination matters when you are buying land near Laporte, Fort Collins, Bellvue, or Wellington. A nearby well can help establish a local expectation, but it does not guarantee the same depth or yield on your lot. Have the permit, construction report, water-level information, and proposed septic layout reviewed before you commit to a building site.

sections.heading: Laporte Well Depth Depends on the Ground Under the Lot
sections.html:
Among wells with reported depths, the median is 40 feet. The middle half falls between 21 and 118 feet, while 72% are under 100 feet. Another 16% are 100 to 300 feet, 9% are 300 to 600 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet. The range is not a typo: the deepest recorded well is 2,340 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 2,027 wells in that category. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through separate cracks, so two neighboring lots may require very different drilling approaches. For a bid, treat 40 feet as a statistical midpoint, not a guaranteed target. Ask the driller to explain the likely casing, grout, access, and extra-footage charges if the first water-bearing fracture is deeper.

sections.heading: What Laporte Wells Produce for Household Use
sections.html:
Reported well yields have a median of 8.2 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 13.8 gallons per minute. The largest group, 65%, produces between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. A further 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 10% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute and 4% report under 1 gallon per minute.

Only 191 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield numbers describe reported wells rather than every permit. A low-yield result is not automatically unusable, because storage and household demand affect how a system performs. Still, a buyer should request the well construction and production records, confirm the legal use of the permit, and have the proposed pump and pressure-tank setup sized to the actual well.

sections.heading: Laporte Water Levels Are Shallow in the Reported Records
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are relatively shallow: the median depth to water is 13 feet, and the middle half is 9 to 26 feet below the surface. Only 78 wells report a static water level, so these figures are useful local context rather than a guarantee for an untested parcel.

The decade comparison shows a median of 11 feet below surface in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper recent median, but the limited reporting means it should not be treated as proof of a broad, dropping water table. Water levels can vary with location, season, pumping, and measurement conditions. Ask for the date and method of any water-level measurement before using it to plan a pump, basement, or excavation.

sections.heading: Laporte Has a Long Permit and Drilling Record
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 2,331 permitted wells within five miles of Laporte, including 1,309 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued across every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the busiest period in the 2010s at 422 permits. The newest permit year in the local records is 2025.

The records list Authorized (Pe, Pg) most often, with 388 wells, followed by Schott Bros. Drilling (Schott, Carl) with 156 and High Desert Irrigation LLC (Hersh, Larry) with 85. Those names show local permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a driller is available for a new job. Before hiring, verify current licensing, insurance, scope, and who will handle the DWR permit and construction report.

sections.heading: A Laporte Well Starts Cheap on Paper and Costs More Finished
sections.html:
Laporte drilling is modeled as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 40 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $2,600 to $4,000. That is only the hole, not a complete operating water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,600 to $16,000 at that median depth. A written bid should separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, pressure tank, electrical work, trenching, water testing, permit work, and any difficult-access charges. Because the deepest local record is 2,340 feet and fractured rock is unpredictable, ask how the price changes if the driller must continue below the planned depth or the first hole does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Yield, Septic Space, and Building Risk
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve direct questions in fractured bedrock. The local records include 4% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and the small number of yield reports means a buyer should not rely on a neighborhood average alone. A pump test, construction report, and water-quality test are more useful than a verbal assurance that a nearby home has water.

Environmental review also matters. Within about ten miles, the mapped records include 67 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 18 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not establish contamination at a particular lot, but they support testing and careful review of the well location. Keep the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house site coordinated. Confirm setbacks and drainage with the county and the applicable DWR permit before excavation.

sections.heading: What to Do Before Buying or Building Near Laporte
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby DWR permits rather than relying on a broad regional estimate. Look for reported depth, yield, static water level, aquifer description, construction details, and the permitted use. Domestic or household use accounts for 52% of local permits, while monitoring wells account for 31%; do not assume every mapped well is a usable household supply.

For a vacant lot, get a driller's site review and a written budget that includes the completed system, not just the per-foot rate. Check whether an exempt household-use well fits the parcel and planned use; Colorado's exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask whether an augmentation plan is required. Before closing, make water testing, septic feasibility, access for a drill rig, and confirmation of the permit conditions part of the review.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Laporte, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Laporte is 40 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 118 feet, and 72% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Conditions vary sharply in fractured granite and gneiss, however; the deepest local record is 2,340 feet. Nearby well depths are useful for planning, not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Laporte?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate for Laporte's fractured mountain bedrock is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $2,600 to $4,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,600 to $16,000. A bid should explain how costs change if the hole must go deeper.

faq.q: How much water does a Laporte well produce?
faq.a: Reported yields have a median of 8.2 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 13.8 gallons per minute. Sixty-five percent of reported yields fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 191 wells report a pump yield, so request the actual construction and production records for the property instead of relying only on the local median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Laporte?
faq.a: Local well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 67 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 18 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a problem at your parcel, but they make a laboratory water test and review of the well location important before purchase or occupancy.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Laporte?
faq.a: Check the DWR permit, construction report, depth, yield, static water level, legal use, and water-quality results. Laporte has 2,331 permitted wells in the local record, but only 1,309 are recorded as constructed and only 191 report a pump yield. Also confirm septic feasibility, drill-rig access, building setbacks, and whether an augmentation plan is needed for the planned use.
